title: Protocol for microplastic pollution monitoring in freshwater ecosystems: Towards a high-throughput sample processing - MICROPLASTREAM
author: de Carvalho, Van-Craynest, et al.

Based on these results, we recommend a double-step digestion and a double stereomicroscope inspection by a different operator in order to facilitate sample inspection and avoid bias in concentration and characteristics while quantifying microplastic pollution. This protocol was optimized for our objectives and the environmental matrix found in river surface water. Further adaptations comprising other matrices and/or microplastic smaller than 700 µm are in perspective. In the case of smaller microplastics and because of the instrumental size limitation of ATR-FTIR, other analytical techniques might be applied to guarantee the unequivocal identification of particle composition, such as micro-FTIR (FTIR combined with an optical microscope), Raman or thermoanalytical methods, e.g. pyrolysis coupled to gas chromatography and mass spectrometry (pyr-GC–MS) [9,30]. In the case of smaller microplastics, it is also important to be careful with mesh size in sampling devices as they can lead to net clogging and underestimation of microplastic pollution [4]. Finally, to ensure the robustness of future microplastic pollution monitoring, we also identify a need to improve our knowledge related to the initial step of the process, i.e. field collection and to fully understand the role of small spatial (i.e. lateral and vertical variability) and temporal (e.g. diurnal changes) variations on our estimate of microplastic pollution.

steps.title: Field sample collection
steps.instruction: Collect surface water with a Manta trawl equipped with a 500 µm mesh, retrieve the cod‑end, filter the collected material through a 500 µm metal sieve, transfer the retained fraction into labelled sealable plastic bags and store the bags at 4 °C until laboratory processing.

steps.title: Initial sample preparation
steps.instruction: In the laboratory, weigh the wet mass of each sample, remove coarse organic/inorganic debris (branches, pebbles, leaves, gravels) and particles larger than 5 mm over a 500 µm sieve while rinsing with distilled water, then transfer the retained material into labelled 250 mL glass bottles.

steps.title: Add potassium hydroxide
steps.instruction: Add potassium hydroxide (KOH) 10 % (w/w) solution (Sigma‑Aldrich pellets) to each bottle at a ratio of 4 mL KOH per 1 g wet sample. If the sample wet mass exceeds 40 g (requiring >160 mL KOH), split the sample into multiple bottles to avoid overflow.

steps.title: KOH digestion incubation
steps.instruction: Place a 5 cm × 5 cm square of 500 µm Nitex tissue on the bottle opening, close with an open‑screw cap, cover the bottle with aluminum foil or tray (inox tray recommended), and incubate in a water bath at 60 °C for 8 h. Monitor temperature with a thermometer placed in a parallel water‑only bottle and check the bath water level every 2 h, refilling as needed.

steps.title: Wash after KOH digestion
steps.instruction: Remove the liquid by pouring it through the Nitex tissue, add 40 mL distilled water through the tissue with a syringe, shake and stir the bottle to enhance washing, then pour off the liquid again. Repeat this wash cycle (remove, add water, shake, remove) at least three times or until the rinsing liquid is clear.

steps.title: Hydrogen peroxide digestion
steps.instruction: Add hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) 30 % (w/w) solution (Merck KGaA) until the sample is fully covered. Handle with care because the mixture becomes highly reactive. Incubate the bottles overnight at room temperature (≈16 h) without heating.

steps.title: Wash after H2O2 digestion
steps.instruction: Perform the same washing sequence as in step 4 (remove liquid, add 40 mL distilled water through the tissue, shake, pour off) repeatedly until the rinsing liquid is clear.

steps.title: Final filtration and storage
steps.instruction: Remove the filter‑cap, place it upside‑down and filter the sample through the Nitex tissue, adding water as needed to rinse all remaining content from the bottle. Transfer the tissue with the retained material into a labelled 8 cm diameter Petri dish and store the dish at room temperature.

steps.title: Stereomicroscope inspection
steps.instruction: Examine the Petri dish under a stereomicroscope (14× magnification suggested), select potential plastic particles and transfer each to a new identified Petri dish. Randomize the order of samples. Repeat the entire inspection with a second operator to reduce bias; this constitutes the second stereomicroscope analysis.

steps.title: Particle documentation and measurement
steps.instruction: Photograph each selected particle together with a ruler or size reference and store the image individually (e.g., in a 96‑well plate kept at room temperature). Categorise particle shape into one of five classes (line, film, fragment, pellet, sphere). Using ImageJ, measure the two orthogonal axes (maximal length and height); estimate width based on shape if required. Weigh each particle to the nearest 0.001 mg and record the mass in the same well‑plate location.

steps.title: ATR‑FTIR chemical identification
steps.instruction: Analyse each particle by ATR‑FTIR spectroscopy, compare its spectrum with an open‑source library and assign a polymer composition only if the library match score is ≥60 %.
